I farm 10.1 mu in Quzhou County. Last year I kept 7.1 mu in wheat-maize and 3 mu in chili, and this year I will do the same because those are the crops I know, and my family can handle the labor. My wheat went in last October after I ran the rotary tiller. Now it is spring, and I will give it the greening water and spread 60 jin of urea per mu on top — that is about 28 kg of urea, giving me roughly 13 kg of nitrogen, plus the 7.5 kg from the one bag of compound fertilizer I put down before sowing, so about 22 kg of nitrogen per mu total. I will irrigate four times: greening, jointing, heading, and grain filling if May turns dry. I spray three times — herbicide once, then fungicide and insecticide once each. If the weather holds I will get 500 kg per mu.

For the summer maize on the same 7.1 mu, I will plant hybrid seeds right after the wheat comes off in early June. I will rotary till once to break the stubble, then sow with 80 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as basal. When the plants reach the big trumpet stage I will spread 50 jin of urea per mu. That is about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu total. Maize does not need much water — I will irrigate twice, once when it is shooting and once when the grain fills, unless the summer rains are good. I spray herbicide at sowing and insecticide once for corn borer, so two pesticide times. I expect 550 kg per mu.

My 3 mu of chili is my cash crop. I will buy hybrid seedlings and plant in late April after rotary tillage. Chili needs heavy feeding. I will put down one and a half bags — 160 jin — of compound fertilizer per mu before planting, then topdress twice with urea and once with potassium sulfate. Total nitrogen will be about 25 kg per mu, phosphorus about 8 kg, potassium about 18 kg. I will irrigate six times because chili cannot dry out. I will spray pesticide every seven to ten days, ten times total, to fight aphids and virus. Chemicals and pumping cost a lot, but last year chili prices were good. I expect 2400 kg per mu of fresh chili.

I worry about money. My son works off-farm in Shijiazhuang and sends some home, but we are saving for his wedding. I would rather spend extra on fertilizer than risk losing yield. A bad harvest is a disaster; wasting half a bag of urea is just a cost. I watch my neighbors. If Lao Wang and the others around me use about the same amounts, then I do too. I do not change my methods unless I see with my own eyes that something works on another farmer's field.
